title: Methodus generalior numeros quosvis satis grandes perscrutandi utrum sint primi necne?

deep.reconstruction:
Top of the page: this finishes an example in which N = 999601 is examined with the idoneal number 840 (N is of the form 840a^2+b^2). A second representation 840x^2+y^2 has been found, so N is composite. Euler builds the fraction p/q = (x±a)/(y±b), which gives four fractions because of the ambiguous signs. From p/q = 1/28 he gets 840·1+28^2 = 1624; divided by 56 this is 15+14 = 29. From p/q = 1/30 he gets 840+900 = 1740; divided by 60 this is 14+15 = 29. From p/q = 41/810 he gets 840·41^2+810^2 = 2068140; divided by 60 this is 14·41^2+27·405 = 34469. Indeed 29·34469 = 999601. This is the standard way to extract a factor from two representations by the same form, taking the gcd through the form value of a suitable rational combination.

§61: Euler stresses that large idoneal numbers are what make it possible to test large numbers. 1848 is the largest idoneal number in his table, so he states a general problem: decide whether N = 1848a^2+b^2 is prime. Naively, one subtracts 1848x^2 for every x and looks for squares. If the only square left is the known one (x = a), N is prime; if another square appears, N is composite and its factors can be assigned.

§63: To reduce the work, write 1848(a^2-x^2) = y^2-b^2. Since 1848 = 8·3·7·11, put y = 22z+b. Then y^2-b^2 = 44z(11z+b), and dividing by 88 gives 21a^2 - ½z(11z+b) = 21x^2. Setting z(11z+b) = 21pq turns this into a^2 - ½pq = x^2. There are four cases, according to how 21 = 3·7 divides between the two factors z and 11z+b:
- I: 11z+b = 21p, z = q.
- II: 11z+b = p, z = 21q.
- III: 11z+b = 7p, z = 3q.
- IV: 11z+b = 3p, z = 7q.

§64: Each linear congruence is solved by Euler's continued-division ('Euclidean') parametrization:
- I: p = 11s-b, q = z = 21s-2b, giving a^2 - ½(11s-b)(21s-2b) = x^2.
- II: q = s, p = 231s+b, z = 21s, giving a^2 - ½s(231s+b) = x^2.
- III: q = 7s-3b, p = 33s-14b, z = 21s-9b, giving a^2 - ½(7s-3b)(33s-14b) = x^2.

Case IV continues on the next page. In every case the search reduces to subtracting a quadratic sequence in s, with constant second difference 231, from a^2. This is far smaller than subtracting multiples of 1848x^2. It is a sieve-like reduction that uses the residue conditions y ≡ ±b modulo 2, 3, 7 and 11.
errors: No arithmetic errors on this page. All of the following check out: 1624/56 = 29, 1740/60 = 29, 2068140/60 = 34469, 29·34469 = 999601, y^2-b^2 = 44z(11z+b) so that dividing by 88 gives the factor ½, and the parametrizations in cases I-III (for example 11(21s-2b)+b = 21(11s-b), and 11(21s-9b)+b = 7(33s-14b)).

Gap (standard for Euler): the criterion 'no other square implies prime' tacitly requires gcd(1848a, b) = 1, and that the representations counted are proper. The setting y = 22z+b fixes y ≡ b (mod 22); the alternative y ≡ -b is covered only by letting b take either sign, which Euler does implicitly (the next page uses 231s ± 197).

ideas.what: Primality test via uniqueness of representation by x^2 + n y^2 with n idoneal (here n = 840 and n = 1848)
ideas.modern_name: Euler's idoneal (convenient) numbers; one class per genus for discriminant -4n
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (idoneal numbers, 1778 papers); theory clarified by Gauss (Disquisitiones, §303)
ideas.where_published: E708, E715, E719 and related papers on numeri idonei (Nova Acta / Opera omnia I.3-4)

ideas.what: Extracting a factor of N from two representations Na^2+b^2 = Nx^2+y^2 via the fraction (x±a)/(y±b) and the form value divided by a common factor
ideas.modern_name: Factorization from two representations by a quadratic form (Euler's factoring method generalized)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (for sums of two squares, 1740s); generalized to x^2 + n y^2 by Euler

ideas.what: Reducing the search space using y ≡ ±b modulo the prime factors of 1848, splitting into four cases by how 3 and 7 divide z and 11z+b, then tabulating quadratic sequences by differences
ideas.modern_name: Congruence sieve / exclusion method (precursor of Gauss's exclusion method and later sieve-type factoring)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler; later Gauss (Disquisitiones, exclusion method), Legendre
ideas.where_published: This paper E719 (Nova Acta 14, 1805) and related idoneal-number papers

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard, well-documented use of the idoneal number 1848 for primality testing, with a routine case split. Euler's idoneal-number primality work, including 1848, is thoroughly treated in the literature (Weil, Opera omnia commentary, Sandifer). Nothing appears uncredited.
transcription_corrections: The fractions after 'Formetur fractio' read p/q = (x±a)/(y±b), followed by four numerical fractions. From the image the first is 1/28 and the fourth is 1/30; the second is 41/810, and the third gives the same factor 34469.
In the first-fraction line the image shows the expression ending in '28^2', divided by 56, giving 15+14 = 29. This is consistent with 840pp+qq.
The '14·41^2+27·405 = 34469' line is correct as transcribed; the product 29·34469 = 999601 is confirmed.
The next page's transcription '(5s+b)(77s+26b)' should read '(3s+b)(77s+26b)', since q = 3s+b in case IV.
